https://www.oedigital.com/news/542006-ro.text: Romania Destroys Drones Drifting Near Offshore Gas Project Published Aug 11, 2026 8:19 pm ET Romanian army divers destroyed two Gerbera-type drones drifting in the country's Black Sea exclusive economic zone near the offshore gas project Neptun Deep, Defence Minister Radu Miruta said on Tuesday. The NATO state shares a 614-km (382-mile) land border with Ukraine and has seen Russian drones repeatedly breach its airspace over the last four years, as well as mines floating in the Black Sea across key trade and energy routes. In July, Romanian F-16 fighter jet pilots shot down three Russian drones breaching national airspace over three consecutive days after dozens of such incursions in the more than four years of Moscow's invasion of Ukraine. On Tuesday, a civilian vessel working near the Neptun Deep offshore gas project spotted the drones, Miruta said. The minister did not specify the origin of the drones, but said Ukraine had confirmed they did not belong to its forces. "For the safety of the shipping lane and the works being carried out around the platform, the decision was made to carry out a controlled destruction by detonation," Miruta said. "The defence ministry contacted Ukrainian partners, who confirmed that the systems do not belong to them." NATO states Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey, which share the Black Sea with Georgia, Russia and Ukraine, have neutralised more than 150 mines drifting across crucial trade lanes. In July, the three states agreed to expand a joint task force that clears mines floating in the Black Sea to include missions to protect critical infrastructure. All three countries have gas exploration or production projects in the Black Sea. Romania's Neptun Deep, jointly owned by OMV Petrom and state gas producer Romgaz, is due to come onstream in 2027 and make Romania the European Union's largest gas producer. https://nineoclock.ro/globinvest-launche.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount SAI Globinvest , one of Romania’s long-standing investment management companies, listed its second ETF today, August 18, on the Regulated Market of the Bucharest Stock Exchange (BVB), under the ticker symbol GIBXTETF. Globinvest BET-XT ETF aims to fully replicate the structure of the BVB’s reference index, BET-XT. Starting August 18, a new ETF is available for trading on the Bucharest Stock Exchange (BVB) Globinvest, a Romanian investment management company with more than 30 years of experience, launches Globinvest BET-XT ETF, which tracks the performance of the BET-XT index The BET-XT index comprises the 30 most traded Romanian companies listed on the BVB Regulated Market Since the beginning of the year, BET-XT has increased by 46% TradeVille, an active participant in the BVB trading system, will act as the issuer’s Market Maker The ETF can be traded on the BVB through authorized brokers, with the full list available HERE The Bucharest Stock Exchange now has a total of 10 ETFs available for trading Launched by the BVB in 2008, BET-XT is a price index that tracks the performance of the 30 most traded Romanian companies listed on the BVB Regulated Market. With a broader composition than the benchmark BET index, it provides a wider perspective on the evolution of the Romanian capital market. The complete composition of the index is available HERE. The total market capitalization of all Romanian companies included in the BET-XT index stands at approximately RON 438 billion, representing 60% of the total market capitalization of the main segment, which exceeded RON 724 billion at the end of the trading day on August 17. Since its launch, BET-XT has increased by 340%. At the same time, the first half of 2026 recorded the index’s strongest H1 performance since its launch. Also in 2026, the BET-XT index surpassed the 3,000-point threshold for the first time, reaching 3,078.66 points following the trading session on August 17. Since the beginning of the year, BET-XT has increased by 46%. “With the launch of Globinvest ‘s second ETF, we reach the milestone of 10 ETFs available for trading on the Bucharest Stock Exchange. This confirms the maturity of our market and the democratization of investing through ETFs. Investors have a simple way to invest in the stock market – they can buy a diversified portfolio without having to perform complex analyses. Capital market development is a joint effort: the result of a partnership between fund managers, listed companies, and investors who put their money to work. With a 46% return for the BET-XT index since the beginning of the year, the outlook remains optimistic. We continue to build a modern stock exchange, open to everyone looking to secure a better financial future,” said Radu Hanga, President of the Bucharest Stock Exchange . “Investors seeking broader exposure to the Romanian capital market now have the opportunity to invest in Globinvest’s new ETF. Diversification across the 30 most traded companies included in the BET-XT index, combined with the low costs associated with ETFs, makes this investment product accessible and suitable for long-term portfolios. We congratulate Globinvest on its continued development of the ETF market at the BVB and for offering Romanians simple, transparent tools that are easy to integrate into their savings process,” said Remus Vulpescu, CEO of the Bucharest Stock Exchange . Globinvest BET-XT ETF is launched by SAI Globinvest , a Romanian investment management company with more than 30 years of experience, founded in Cluj-Napoca. Within 16 months, Globinvest has launched two ETFs on the BVB, the first being Globinvest Energy & Financials ETF, launched in April 2025. “Globinvest BET-XT ETF is the second ETF launched by Globinvest on the Bucharest Stock Exchange. The BET-XT index components include representative companies from key sectors of the Romanian economy, such as financial, energy, pharmaceutical, industrial, and utilities. Today’s launch represents, at the same time, a vote of confidence: confidence in Romanian companies, confidence in the Bucharest Stock Exchange, confidence in investors and our 2 partners, as well as confidence in the Globinvest team. Through this new product, we are turning the BET-XT index into a genuine, accessible, and liquid investment vehicle,” said Ilie Cenan, President of Globinvest. The ETF benefits from liquidity provider (market maker) services provided by TradeVille, which also handled the admission of the ETF fund units under the ticker symbol GIBXTETF to the BVB Regulated Market. “The listing of GIBXTETF represents a new step in the development of the local ETF market and offers investors access, through a single instrument, to the performance of the top 30 most traded companies on the BVB Regulated Market, reunited under the BET-XT index. We are glad that TradeVille contributed to the completion of this project by assuming the roles of Authorized Participant and Market Maker. By ensuring liquidity, we aim to facilitate the trading of fund units and contribute to the efficient operation of the secondary market. We thank the teams at Globinvest and the Bucharest Stock Exchange, as well as all partners involved, for their collaboration and trust,” said Iulia Ogescu, Capital Market Lawyer at TradeVille . Alongside Globinvest BET-XT ETF, investors currently have access to 9 other ETFs tradable on the Bucharest Stock Exchange. https://www.politico.eu/article/russia-t.text: BRUSSELS — A U.S.-based data-extraction firm accused of being secretly run from Russia has worked on EU-backed projects and sold its services to European law enforcement agencies, according to documents seen by POLITICO. The U.S. Justice Department last week charged Oxygen Forensics — officially headquartered in Virginia — of concealing that it was actually owned and operated by Russians. The company develops and sells powerful software capable of extracting and analyzing information from smartphones and computers, a process known as "digital forensics." According to public records reviewed by POLITICO, Oxygen was used in at least two EU-funded projects aimed at improving how electronic evidence is collected, processed and shared in criminal investigations. Advertisement Advertisement The first project, EVIDENCE, (European Informatics Data Exchange Framework for Courts and Evidence), which received more than €1.9 million in EU funding between 2014 and 2016, listed Oxygen Forensics among the companies consulted on how Europe could better handle and exchange digital criminal evidence. That placed the company in a wider network that included EU police agency Europol, judicial cooperation agency Eurojust and the European Anti-Fraud Office's digital forensics unit. The second project, INSPECTr, backed under Horizon 2020, an EU research and innovation funding arm, was designed to help European police bring together and analyze digital evidence collected using different tools. It built software that could take evidence extracted with Oxygen Forensics and make it easier for investigators using other systems to access and analyze it. Although both of those EU-backed projects were launched well before Russia’s February 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine and subsequent European sanctions, INSEPCTr continued to operate until 2023. Oxygen also currently remains listed on the websites of both projects. On its own now-defunct website, Oxygen Forensics had listed the European Commission as a client. A Commission spokesperson stressed that Oxygen Forensics was not a member of either consortium, "and hence did not receive funding under these projects from the Commission." The spokesperson, who was granted anonymity to speak freely about a sensitive topic, said EU-funded projects are subject to strict eligibility and ethics standards, and "since the beginning of the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine, Russian-based entities cannot participate in Horizon Europe projects in any capacity." Sister company's FSB link More recently, after its involvement with the EU-backed projects, Oxygen's products have been accredited and purchased by multiple national police agencies across Europe, including those in Germany, Spain, Italy and Poland, according to notices in the EU tender database. A statement published Wednesday by the U.S. Justice Department found Oxygen Forensic's software was developed and managed by a team in Russia under the direction of Russian national Oleg Sergeyevich Davydov, but purported to be led by Lee Reiber, a 55-year-old native of Boise, Idaho. An affidavit filed with the complaint says Oxygen Forensics was in contact with the U.S. Department of War and several parts of the Department of Homeland Security, including the Secret Service, its digital-forensics training institute, Homeland Security Investigations and the department's internal watchdog. Advertisement Advertisement Reiber has since been arrested in the U.S. Davydov was arrested Sunday at London's Heathrow Airport as he prepared to board a flight to Istanbul, according to a statement by the Justice Department. Lawyers for the two men did not respond to POLITICO's request for comment. Representatives for Oxygen Forensics did not respond to requests for comment either. In the meantime, the company's website has been seized by the U.S. government. Prosecutors allege that after Washington imposed sanctions on Russia in 2022, Oxygen's Russian owners concealed both their ownership and the continued development of the company's software in Russia. The five Russians behind Oxygen Forensics also controlled a Russian sister company, MKO Systems, that sold the same underlying technology to the Russian Security Service (FSB) and the country's Interior Ministry. The Justice Department complaint does not allege that Oxygen's software contained malicious code or that the company used it to gain unauthorized access to customers' systems or data. U.S. investigators did, however, seize corporate bank accounts, 57 domains and other cyber infrastructure they said was "used in furtherance of the alleged acts." Used across Europe Oxygen's footprint extends beyond the Commission-backed research projects. The French investigative news organization, Disclose, found its surveillance software was supplied to Moroccan authorities under an EU-funded border-management program for the Maghreb. As well as financing the purchase of the software, the EU also funded training courses led by employees of Oxygen Forensics for Moroccan police. The company has listed major European law-enforcement bodies among its customers. Advertisement Advertisement In Hungary, a government procurement document shows that the Hungarian police signed an IT contract in Dec. 2024 with Oxygen Forensics worth 10.14 million Hungarian forints (€27,000) which ran through Dec. 2025. In Italy, an April 2026 technical brief issued by the Public Prosecutor's Office in the Sardinian city of Sassari explicitly lists Oxygen Forensics among the recognized systems that judicial police can use to extract and analyze data from mobile devices. And in Spain, a 2026 study on digital analysis of WhatsApp on Android and Apple smartphones was produced by a National Police inspector accredited by Oxygen Forensics and involved in training police investigators in digital analysis. Law enforcement agencies in Romania and Latvia also bought its software, as recently as September. None of the national police agencies involved responded to requests for comment. Natalia Krapiva, senior legal counsel at digital rights group Access Now, said civil society organizations had warned for years about Oxygen Forensics' Russian ownership and development links, which she said have now been corroborated by the U.S. case. "If in fact Russian-made software designed for the FSB and Investigative Committee was used for handling EU Commission criminal evidence database, it raises a serious possibility of sensitive information being compromised and accessed by Russian authorities," Krapiva said. "We call on the EU and every government using these tools to suspend them and fully investigate how a Russian-owned company spent a decade inside Western law enforcement." https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Nikita Hand. ‘I get so many beautiful messages online. And then I would get the odd hate message, from women and men, just calling me names, horrible names.’ Photograph: Patrick Bolger/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Nikita Hand. ‘I get so many beautiful messages online. And then I would get the odd hate message, from women and men, just calling me names, horrible names.’ Photograph: Patrick Bolger/The Guardian Ireland Interview ‘I wanted to change the stigma’: Nikita Hand on winning her civil rape case against Conor McGregor Rory Carroll in Dublin The popularity of Hand’s book Not the Perfect Victim is the latest twist in a story that puts the spotlight on how society responds to sexual assault allegations Wed 14 Oct 2026 06.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Nikita Hand had a compelling reason to not pursue a civil rape case against Conor McGregor . She was, in her own view, an imperfect victim. The day of the assault, she had been partying with alcohol and cocaine before contacting McGregor, who took her to a Dublin hotel. Hours later, bruised and stunned, Hand made a report to police, but Irish authorities declined to pursue a criminal case against the mixed martial artist, saying there was no reasonable prospect of a conviction. That left the option of a civil case. But that would strip the hairdresser of anonymity, and pit her against a powerful celebrity who denied wrongdoing and had teams of lawyers and a vast online following. Hand went for it. “I’m not the perfect victim and I never portrayed myself to be,” she said in an interview in Dublin. “But I feel when victims are not perfect, they seem to get blamed. And I really wanted to try to change the stigma around people thinking you have to be a perfect victim to be believed or heard.” The cross-examination in the witness box at Dublin high court in 2024 felt like another violation, but Hand emerged victorious : the jury found that McGregor had assaulted her in 2018 and awarded nearly €250,000 in damages. View image in fullscreen Women at a solidarity demonstration in Dublin after Nikita Hand won her case against Conor McGregor in November 2024. Photograph: Cillian Sherlock/PA “I felt vindicated. It was a really happy, special moment, but at the same time it was a really scary moment. It didn’t take away the fear and the anxiety – to this day I still live with the anxiety and the fear.” Hand, 37, has published a book, Not the Perfect Victim , that chronicles the assault and the aftermath of a case that continues to reverberate on both sides of the Atlantic. Jimmy Fallon triggered an outcry in June after hosting McGregor on The Tonight Show for a softball interview. Fallout from the case continued to play out on social media, said Hand. “I get so many beautiful messages online. And then I would get the odd hate message, from women and men, just calling me names, horrible names.” Hand’s appearance on the Irish bestseller list is the latest twist in a story that has put a spotlight on how the legal system, and popular culture, responds to allegations of sexual assault. Hand said she still struggled with being in the public eye, but was proud of the book. “I feel like I’m in control of my own story now, which I felt like I wasn’t for many years. The night of the assault, I wasn’t in control, another person was controlling my body.” View image in fullscreen Ruth Coppinger and Natasha O’Brien take part in a solidarity demonstration in Dublin in 2024 after Nikita Hand won her case against Conor McGregor. Photograph: Cillian Sherlock/PA Growing up in Drimnagh, a west Dublin suburb, Hand had acquaintances in common with McGregor, who was from nearby Crumlin. While he found fame and fortune in and out of the octagon, she worked in a salon as a colourist. In 2018 she had a partner, a five-year-old daughter and a new house. “Life was good. I was bubbly and loved going out with my friends.” At a Christmas work party she drank, took cocaine and, on a whim, messaged McGregor on Instagram, asking if he knew of any parties. He collected Hand and a friend on the morning of 9 December and took them to the Beacon hotel. Hand later testified that McGregor pinned her down on the bed, put her in a headlock and mock-choked her while raping her. Hand went to the home of her mother, who called an ambulance and insisted that Hand report the assault, regardless of McGregor’s status. “She didn’t care who it was. She just cared about her daughter. She’s seen the bruises on me, she’s seen the state I was in.” Hand was examined at a sexual assault treatment unit and gave a statement to police. When questioned, McGregor said the sex was consensual. In 2020 prosecutors decided to not press charges. After failing to reverse that decision Hand took a civil case. “I did want this person to go to jail for what he had done to me but I had no other option but to take up a civil case. Unfortunately, when you have a civil case and you win it, your perpetrator gets to walk free. But I knew I had to do everything in my power to get some sort of justice.” In June 2024, four months before the trial, three masked intruders broke into her home , smashed windows and stabbed her partner. Hand’s lawyers said they believed it was an attack by McGregor supporters, but that McGregor had nothing to do with it. The two-week trial in November 2024 drew intense media attention. The public gallery was packed and Hand was seated almost within touching distance of McGregor. The cross-examination was humiliating, she said. “I found it really degrading. I found it just as bad as the assault itself. Sometimes I feel like victims nearly are on trial rather than the perpetrators. That’s the way we’re kind of made to feel.” McGregor lost an appeal in July 2025. Last month a Dublin couple, Samantha O’Reilly and Steven Cummins, were charged with perjury after an investigation by police into evidence filed in McGregor’s appeal. View image in fullscreen Nikita Hand in Dublin in September. Photograph: Patrick Bolger/The Guardian Hand credits her mother, her partner and the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre with helping her to rebuild her life and to accept that the assault was not her fault. “The shame is leaving me but I do have my really bad days when I can’t leave my apartment. I have severe anxiety.” She is no longer a hairdresser. “I did try to go back to work and it just wasn’t the same. So it will be a complete career change for me. I’d love to work with victims and survivors and help them have a voice.” She wants her daughters – a teenager and a newborn – to grow up in a world where victims are not shamed or blamed. “It doesn’t matter what you wear or how much you drink or even take a drug. No means no and consent needs to be taken more seriously.” Hand said McGregor should not have been hosted at the White House in 2025 or on Fallon’s chatshow. “It’s really upsetting. I can’t understand how he’s still given such a huge platform.” She seldom mentions McGregor by name. “I don’t have any feelings for him. I don’t forgive him. I gave my evidence, he gave his and the jury made their decision. And that’s all there is to it.” Explore more on these topics Ireland Conor McGregor Rape and sexual assault MMA Europe interviews Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

http://www.russiaherald.com/news/2793496.text: 'Like African Americans during segregation': How Russians became second-class 'non-citizens' inside the EU RT.com 03 Oct 2026, 22:40 GMT+10 As Latvia votes, its largest minority faces shrinking language rights, fractured representation, and little hope of a political reset Latvia's Russian-speaking population has reached a point that human rights advocates describe as critical. The country has completed its transition to Latvian-only education, Russian has all but disappeared from public communication, and the institution of 'non-citizens' - ethnic Russians denied a range of rights - remains in place. But on October 3, Latvia elects a new Saeima (parliament). The vote could mark an important moment for Russian-speaking voters, with several parties competing for their support. Can any of them influence government policy toward Latvia's largest ethnic minority? Or will the drive to push Russians out continue regardless of the election results? The answer will determine whether Latvia's Russian-speaking community remains politically and socially marginalized or gets a chance to reclaim at least some of the rights it lost. How the status of Russians changed The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 radically changed the position of Russians in Latvia. Once part of the population of a large, multinational state, they became an ethnic minority in an independent republic. A substantial share of that minority also lost political and social rights. One of the pivotal decisions was the introduction of 'non-citizen' status. Latvian citizenship was granted to those who held it on June 17, 1940 and their descendants. Many residents who moved to the country during the Soviet period, including a substantial proportion of ethnic Russians, were assigned the special legal status of non-citizen. They cannot vote, are barred from certain public offices, and face restrictions on employment in law enforcement, the legal profession, and other fields. "The situation facing Latvia's Russian-speaking population is grim. Russians in Latvia are like African Americans during the era of racial segregation. They have been stripped of a substantial range of rights. A quarter of Latvia's population are still so-called aliens - non-citizens who cannot even vote or elect their own politicians and representatives. Russians are almost entirely absent from government. Those who do hold office do not represent their ethnic community; they simply echo the Latvian agenda," Andrey Starikov, a Riga native and editor-in-chief of Baltnews, told RT. Language, schools, and cultural life Access to education in their native language remains one of the most painful issues for Russian-speaking residents. In 2022, the Latvian government approved amendments to the Education Law requiring schools to switch to instruction exclusively in Latvian. Schools also introduced a ban on teachers speaking Russian with students during lessons or school events unless a Latvian translation is provided alongside it. Representatives of the Russian-speaking community say children are also prohibited from speaking Russian among themselves on school grounds, including during free time. Russian is gradually disappearing from public life as well. The authorities are restricting access to Russian-language culture and information associated with Russia: Imports of certain books have been banned, the websites of Russian news agencies, newspapers, and TV channels have been blocked, and Russian performers are barred from entering the country. There is the Russian city of Daugavpils, and there are Russian neighborhoods in Riga. Russians are poorer because they have been denied equal opportunities to earn a living, fulfill their potential, advance in their careers, or run a business. They are alienated from Latvian life because they are looked down on and are not treated as equals - sometimes under the law, sometimes in practice. They face a whole host of restrictions," Starikov said. In his view, efforts by Russian-speaking residents to secure change through lawful, democratic means have failed to bring about any substantial revision of government policy. Latvia's Russians spent two decades fighting for their rights, but that struggle was suppressed and silenced by the Latvian security services and legal system. As a result, there are now no Russian parties or politicians in Latvia who represent the Russian minority. Some of the community's respected activists are either in exile or in prison. Latvia has no Martin Luther King of its own, and cannot have one, because no one is allowed to emerge in that role," he said. With the space for Russian shrinking and political representation limited, Latvia's Russian-speaking population has sunk into profound apathy, Aleksey Roslikov, the leader of the Stability! party and a candidate for the Saeima, told RT. "The apathy among Russian speakers has grown many times worse. Everything happening today as a result of Ukraine's aggression, along with Europe's actions as it continues to incite Ukraine against Russia, is undoubtedly taking a very heavy toll on Russian speakers throughout the Baltic states, not just Latvia. All Russian speakers have now been branded enemies and traitors. The situation with education and the language ban... Russians have sunk into deep apathy, and it will be extremely difficult to find a way out." What the election holds for Russians Latvia heads into the 2026 election, for the first time, without a single dominant 'Russian party' of the old kind - a party capable of acting as an intermediary between Russian-speaking voters and the state. Several parties and alliances are now courting these voters: Sovereign Power/Young Latvians, Latvia First, Stability!, and Harmony Center. Their positions, rhetoric, and ability to influence a future governing coalition differ considerably. Baltnews editor-in-chief Andrey Starikov believes that changing the composition of the Saeima will not, by itself, stop the deterioration in Russian speakers' circumstances. "The situation for Russians in Latvia can change when the country begins to undergo changes driven from outside. Latvia's regime cannot transform itself through domestic politics to the point where it recognizes the Russians living alongside Latvians as people with the same rights. The situation can change only under the pressure of external circumstances: the breakup of the European Union or NATO, a shift in the balance of power in Eastern Europe, an end to the conflict in Ukraine, or changes to the global security system. Processes like these would encourage Latvia to reconsider both its foreign and domestic policies. Nothing can be changed from outside through democratic procedures. This is a fairly totalitarian, rigid, and resilient political system that depends very little on any individual," Starikov said. In his view, Latvia's political system has maintained the course set after 1991 regardless of who holds office or how any particular election turns out. "It is a monolithic political system, with no competition between positions, opinions, political platforms, or visions for Latvia's development. Elections here are a formality, a ritual. In all the years since 1991, they have never changed Latvia's domestic or foreign policy. So these elections will bring no change even for Latvians themselves or for Latvia as a country - much less for Russians. This is simply political theater, a political ritual," Starikov said. Roslikov takes a more optimistic view. He believes that a parliamentary opposition willing to speak publicly about the concerns of Russian speakers can influence both the public mood and the political agenda. "We understand that when there is an opposition in parliament - an opposition that defends the interests and rights of Russians and Russian speakers in Latvia - it has an extremely positive effect, and its influence extends beyond Latvia to Lithuania and Estonia. I, for example, have enormous support throughout the Baltic states. There is a reason the Estonians have declared me a national security threat and barred me from entering their country. This is direct evidence that when an ethnic group has representatives at the highest levels of government who actually defend that community, the mood begins to change and people gain strength." The outlook ahead of the vote According to a forecast by the Latvian polling organization SKDS, the United List bloc, led by Latvia's incumbent prime minister, Andris Kulbergs, is leading the race. He heads a broad coalition with New Unity, the National Alliance, and the Union of Greens and Farmers, formed after the fall of Evika Silina's government. The poll puts the bloc's potential share of the vote at 14.4%. In second place, with 9.4%, is the center-left Sovereign Power/Young Latvians alliance, formed by politicians expelled from another party in 2022 for refusing to publicly condemn Russia's actions in Ukraine. The alliance hopes to attract votes from the ethnic Russian minority. Next comes the center-right Latvia First party, with 9.2%. Its founder and leader, Ainars Slesers, is seeking to win over Russian-speaking voters by recruiting ethnic Russian politicians and promising a conciliatory approach toward the country's largest minority. The remaining parties are: the Progressives at 6.2%, the National Alliance at 5.6%, the Union of Greens and Farmers at 4.8%, New Unity at 4.3%, Stability! at 2.8%, We Change the Rules at 2.5%, For Latvia's Development at 2.4%, and Harmony Center at 2%. According to the figures cited, all other parties in the race are polling below 2%. Parties must clear the 5% threshold to enter parliament. "At the moment, my party has fairly good chances," Roslikov told RT. "But we fully understand that Europe does not count votes honestly. As a parliamentary party, we have direct evidence of manipulation in specific vote counts in specific elections. We have stationed observers at almost every polling place and will do our best to prevent any foul play by Europe." Little hope for change Both of RT's interviewees agree that Russian speakers should not expect major changes after the election. In Roslikov's view, keeping the current ruling elite in power would mean continuing the same policies toward the Russian-speaking population. "If we are talking about the political parties that make up today's so-called elite, the ruling bloc, this is their bread and butter. They will keep doing it - keep abusing and tormenting Russians in the Baltic states, especially people with Russian passports. There is no hope for change, and there can be none." Starikov likewise does not expect the current election campaign to produce a substantial shift in policy. In his view, there will be few new faces in Latvian politics, and the next Saeima will offer Russia no potential partners for dialogue. "Nevertheless, Russia should still pay attention to this process. It is another opportunity to document the appalling situation facing Latvia's Russian population in terms of rights and freedoms, to offer our assessment once again, and to address that community and repeat: 'We are waiting for you. Come to Russia. There is no ultranationalism in Russia. Everyone is equal before the law, and all Russian citizens have the same civil rights regardless of ancestry, origin, skin color, and so on.'" Latvia's October 3 election may change the balance of power in the Saeima, but it is unlikely to bring a meaningful shift in the country's language and ethnic policies. Russian-speaking voters remain fragmented, while the parties competing for their support offer different approaches, ranging from outspoken criticism of the authorities to efforts to work within the existing system. For Latvia's Russian residents, the outcome will not be decisive. Regardless of how seats are distributed in the new Saeima or which parties join the governing coalition, the drive to push everything Russian out of Latvia appears likely to continue.
